Abstract—Although the technology of flash memory is rapidly improving, SSD usage is still limited due to the high cost per storage capacity. In such a case, improving the storage utilization is the critical issue to achieve the desirable system performance. In this paper, we propose an extent-based allocation scheme for hybrid storage solutions, called MatBall (Matrix and extent-based allocation), whose objective is to increase space utilization of SSD partition in the hybrid file system by reducing fragmentation overhead. In MatBall, to consume the remaining spaces as much as possible posterior to file allocations, I/O units (extents) of the hybrid file system are recursively partitioned into segments in the subsequent level and further file allocations are performed in units of the partitioned segments. The performance measurement with IOzone shows that the hybrid file system using MatBall enables to produce higher bandwidth over ext2 installed on HDD and SSD.
Keywords-component; extent partitioning, matrix-based allocation, file mapping, fragmentation overhead
I. INTRODUCTION
Many file systems have been developed for the purpose of optimizing the moving overhead of HDD disk arms in I/O operations. However, as the new technology, such as SSD (Solid State Device), rapidly improved, the file system research for integrating those technologies into the storage capacity has become received the great attention because they possess the promising performance characteristics to satisfy the need of commercial applications. Especially, SSD that uses flash memory as the storage medium is considered the next-generation storage device, due to its advantages such as high random I/O and non-volatility [1-4]
However, the key obstacle to the widening SSD adoption to large-scale storage subsystems is its high cost per capacity, compared to that of HDD. Even though the cost of flash memory becomes decrease, the price of SSD is still much higher and such a high cost/capacity ratio makes it less desirable to construct large-scale storage subsystems solely composed of SSD devices.
There are several ways of utilizing SSD advantages to boost I/O performance $[5-8]$ . The first one is to implement SSD-related I/O optimizations in the file system level. For example, DFS $[6]$ uses fusion-io ioDrive to provide the virtualization flash storage layer that acts as the traditional block device driver with FTL. Also, F2FS [7] proposed a new filesystem metadata platform that can reduce SSD-specific semiconductor overheads.
Although those file systems have successfully integrated SSDs to improve I/O performance, adapting a new file system to the existing storage solutions is not easy because it should go through the long, pains-taking process to prove the durable data consistency and reliability.
An alternative is to use hybrid storage subsystems, which are managed by the hybrid file system or SSD-specific cache $[9,10]$ . In such methods, a small portion of SSD partition is combined with a much larger HDD storage capacity in a cost-effective way, while making use of the strengths of both devices. Since only a small-size of file system address space is provided by SSD partition, increasing space utilization for SSD partition has a critical impact in improving I/O performance.
In this paper, we propose an extent-based file allocation approach, called MatBall. The primary objective of MatBall is to increase the usage of the costly SSD storage resources as much as possible in the hybrid file system, by reusing the remaining spaces of I/O units and thus by decreasing fragmentation overhead. In the hybrid file system where the entire address spaces are constructed on both SSD and HDD partitions, MatBall can contribute to maximize the space usage of SSD partition by taking responsibility of allocating files in SSD partition.
The rest of paper is organized as follows: In section II, we present the implementation details of MatBall. The performance results of MatBall integrated with the hybrid file system are shown in Section III. In Section IV, we conclude our paper.

**Abstract—** Although flash memory technology is advancing rapidly, solid-state drives (SSDs) are still not widely adopted for large-scale storage due to their high cost per gigabyte. This makes efficient use of SSD space a critical challenge—every bit of performance advantage we gain from SSDs can be wasted if we don’t use their storage capacity wisely. In this paper, we introduce a new file allocation strategy called **MatBall (Matrix and extent-based allocation)**, designed specifically for hybrid storage systems that combine SSDs and traditional hard disk drives (HDDs). The goal? To squeeze every last drop of usable space out of the limited SSD partition by minimizing **fragmentation overhead**—the wasted gaps that form when files are stored inefficiently.

So how does MatBall do this? Instead of treating each file allocation as a fixed block, MatBall breaks down I/O units—called *extents*—into smaller, flexible pieces called *segments*. After a file is written, any leftover space isn’t just left behind. Instead, MatBall recursively subdivides these extents into smaller segments at deeper levels, allowing future small files or file fragments to fit neatly into the gaps. It’s like packing a suitcase: instead of leaving awkward empty spaces after placing large items, you use smaller boxes to fill in the corners. This dynamic segmentation dramatically improves space utilization on the SSD.

We tested MatBall using **IOzone**, a standard benchmarking tool for file system performance. The results show that a hybrid file system using MatBall achieves higher data transfer bandwidth than **ext2**—a classic Linux file system—running directly on either HDD or SSD alone. This means faster reads and writes, better responsiveness, and more efficient use of expensive SSD storage.

### I. INTRODUCTION

For decades, file systems were designed around the physical limitations of **hard disk drives (HDDs)**—especially the time it takes for the read/write head to move across spinning platters. These mechanical delays shaped how data was organized, with strategies focused on minimizing disk arm movement and grouping related data together.

But times have changed. **Solid-state drives (SSDs)**, which store data on flash memory chips with no moving parts, offer game-changing advantages: lightning-fast random access, lower latency, and higher durability. Because of these benefits, SSDs are now seen as the future of storage, especially for performance-critical applications like databases, cloud services, and real-time analytics [1–4].

Yet, despite their speed, SSDs come with a major drawback: **cost per gigabyte**. Even as prices drop, SSDs remain significantly more expensive than HDDs for the same amount of storage. This makes it impractical to build large-scale storage systems using only SSDs—at least for now.

So what’s the solution? One promising approach is **hybrid storage**: combining a small, fast SSD with a large, cheap HDD. Think of it like a sports car parked in your garage—you don’t drive it all the time, but when you need speed, it’s there. In a hybrid system, frequently accessed or performance-sensitive data lives on the SSD, while bulk, less-critical data stays on the HDD.

But here’s the catch: since the SSD portion is small, **we must use every byte of it as efficiently as possible**. If we waste space due to poor file allocation, we lose the performance benefits we’re trying to gain. That’s where **fragmentation** becomes a serious problem.

Fragmentation happens when files are stored in non-contiguous chunks, leaving behind scattered pockets of unused space too small to be useful. On HDDs, fragmentation mainly hurts performance because of increased seek time. But on SSDs, especially in a hybrid setup, **space fragmentation directly reduces how much data we can store on the fast tier**, limiting the system’s overall effectiveness.

There are several ways researchers have tried to leverage SSDs for better I/O performance [5–8]. One approach is to design entirely new file systems optimized for flash memory. For example:

- **DFS [6]** uses high-performance SSDs like Fusion-io ioDrive to create a virtualized flash layer that mimics a traditional block device, relying on Flash Translation Layer (FTL) for wear leveling and address mapping.
- **F2FS (Flash-Friendly File System) [7]** rethinks file system metadata structures to reduce internal SSD overheads like garbage collection and write amplification.

These systems work well, but there’s a big barrier: **adopting a new file system is risky and time-consuming**. Enterprises need strong guarantees about data integrity, crash consistency, and long-term reliability. Proving all of that takes years of testing and real-world validation—something most organizations aren’t ready to invest in lightly.

That’s why **hybrid storage subsystems** are gaining traction. Instead of replacing existing file systems, they enhance them. These systems either use a **hybrid file system** or an **SSD-specific cache** [9,10] to intelligently place data across SSD and HDD. A small SSD acts as a performance booster—like a turbocharger—while the bulk of storage remains on affordable HDDs.

In such setups, only a fraction of the total address space resides on the SSD. Therefore, **maximizing SSD space utilization isn’t just helpful—it’s essential**. If we can reduce fragmentation and pack more data into the SSD without wasting space, we get faster access to more files, better throughput, and a smarter use of resources.

This is exactly where **MatBall** comes in.

MatBall is an **extent-based file allocation scheme** designed to maximize SSD space usage in hybrid file systems. Its core idea is simple but powerful: instead of allocating entire extents (large blocks of contiguous space) as indivisible units, MatBall allows them to be **dynamically partitioned into smaller segments**. When a file is written and doesn’t fill an entire extent, the leftover space isn’t abandoned. Instead, MatBall recursively divides the extent into smaller and smaller segments, enabling future allocations to reuse those fragments.

Imagine you're organizing shelves in a library. Normally, you might assign one full shelf (an extent) to each book series. But if a series only needs half a shelf, the other half sits empty. With MatBall, you’d split that half into smaller slots and use them for single-volume books. You keep subdividing as needed, making sure no shelf space goes to waste.

By managing file placement at multiple levels of granularity, MatBall reduces both internal and external fragmentation. And because it operates primarily within the SSD partition of a hybrid file system—where space is scarce and valuable—it has an outsized impact on overall performance.

The rest of this paper is organized as follows:  
In **Section II**, we dive deep into the implementation of MatBall, explaining how extent partitioning works, how segments are managed, and how the system decides when and how to subdivide.  
In **Section III**, we present performance measurements using IOzone, showing how MatBall improves bandwidth compared to traditional file systems.  
In **Section IV**, we conclude with a summary of our findings and potential directions for future work.

### II. IMPLEMENTATION DETAILS

#### A. System Model

In MatBall, the fundamental unit of I/O is called an **extent**. But unlike in traditional file systems where an extent is treated as a single, indivisible block of contiguous storage, MatBall treats extents as **composite structures** made up of smaller units called **segments**.

Why do this? Because treating large extents as atomic units leads to **internal fragmentation**—wasted space inside an allocated block. For example, if your extent size is 1 MB but you only need to store a 100 KB file, you end up reserving 900 KB that no other file can use. That’s a huge waste, especially on expensive SSD storage.

To solve this, MatBall performs allocations **not in full extents, but in segments**—smaller, fixed-size chunks that make up an extent. This allows finer-grained control over space usage. When a file is written, it gets assigned one or more segments, not necessarily a whole extent. And when space remains after an allocation, instead of leaving it unusable, MatBall can **recursively partition** the remaining portion into smaller segments at a deeper level, making it available for future allocations.

Let’s break this down step by step:

Suppose an extent consists of 64 blocks. Rather than using all 64 blocks at once, MatBall views this extent as a **hierarchical structure**—like a tree—where each node represents a segment of a certain size. At the top level (Level 0), the entire extent is one big segment. If a file doesn’t need the full 64 blocks, the system can split this top-level segment into two halves (Level 1), each of 32 blocks. If one of those halves is still too big, it can be split again into 16-block segments (Level 2), and so on.

This recursive subdivision continues until we reach a minimum segment size—say, 4 blocks. At that point, we stop splitting and allocate the smallest usable unit.

This approach is similar to **binary buddy memory allocation**, but adapted for file system extents. It ensures that space is reused efficiently, and fragmentation is kept to a minimum.

So MatBall only considers reusing extents that have at least $ \lambda $ contiguous free blocks. When a segment is too big (≥ $ \lambda $), the system splits it in half—this is recursive binary partitioning. Each split creates two smaller segments, and this process can continue down multiple levels, just like dividing a piece of paper in half repeatedly. The maximum number of times you can split a segment of size $ s $ until each piece is smaller than $ \lambda $ is $ \log_2(s / \lambda) $. This logarithmic behavior is crucial—it means even if your storage grows exponentially, the number of steps needed to find the right spot grows very slowly. Therefore, the overall time complexity of Algorithm 1 is $ O(\log_2 s) $, which is highly efficient. Even for large extents, the system quickly narrows down the correct location for the next file. Importantly, in MatBall, **only extents containing at least $ \lambda $ free blocks are reused**. This policy ensures good space utilization by avoiding fragmentation from tiny, scattered free regions. It's a smart trade-off: a little extra computation during allocation prevents much worse inefficiencies later. --- ## III. PERFORMANCE EVALUATION ### A. Experimental Platform To test how well MatBall works in practice, we integrated it into a **hybrid file system**—a clever setup that combines the best of two types of storage: fast Solid-State Drives (SSD) and high-capacity, lower-cost Hard Disk Drives (HDD). Think of this like having a small, ultra-fast express lane (SSD) alongside a large, slower highway (HDD). The entire file system address space is built by merging a small portion of SSD with a much larger portion of HDD. This allows frequently accessed or performance-critical data to live on the SSD, while bulk data resides on the HDD. Here’s how file allocation differs between the two: - On the **HDD partition**, the system uses I/O kernel modules borrowed from **ext2**, a classic Unix file system. Files are allocated one block at a time, which can be slow due to many small I/O operations. - On the **SSD partition**, however, **MatBall takes charge**. Instead of allocating single blocks, MatBall allocates files in **extents**—contiguous groups of segments. This is like moving entire boxes of books at once instead of carrying them one by one. Larger I/O units mean fewer operations and better performance, especially on SSDs that excel at sequential writes. When the hybrid file system is mounted (i.e., made available for use), two important things happen in memory: 1. All **clean extents**—those not yet used for any file—are identified and tracked. 2. The **allocation matrices**, which keep track of which segments are free or occupied, are loaded into memory for fast access. During I/O operations, requests are sent to both the SSD and HDD partitions simultaneously. As soon as **either** partition completes its part of the operation, control returns to the user. This design improves responsiveness, leveraging the SSD’s speed even when the HDD is still working. IOzone Experiment In this experiment, we focused on **write performance**, which is often a bottleneck in storage systems. We used the command: ``` ./iozone -azi -e -g 256M -q 8K ``` Let’s break that down: - `-a`: auto-mode, tests all combinations of record and file sizes. - `-z`: tests a range of file sizes. - `-i`: specifies which tests to run (here, all I/O operations). - `-g 256M`: maximum file size is 256 megabytes. - `-q 8K`: I/O record size is fixed at 8 kilobytes. This setup lets us measure how MatBall performs as file sizes grow from **64KB to 256MB**, under realistic small-write conditions. To eliminate the confounding effect of memory caching (which could make everything seem faster), we called `fsync()` after every I/O operation. This forces data to be written all the way to physical storage, giving us a true picture of disk-level performance. Additionally, we varied the **segment partitioning threshold $ \lambda $** from **16 to 32 blocks** to study its impact on overhead. Larger $ \lambda $ values reduce the number of segments eligible for reuse, which may decrease fragmentation but could also limit allocation flexibility. When comparing **MatBall with 64KB extents** to **ext2 on SSD**, we see about a **19% improvement in write throughput** for 256MB files. Where does this gain come from? The answer lies in **large I/O granularity**. MatBall allocates data in large, contiguous extents, which allows the system to issue fewer, larger write commands. This reduces I/O overhead and keeps the SSD pipeline full—much more efficient than writing one tiny block at a time. This advantage becomes even clearer when we increase the extent size to **256KB**. If you allocate a 64KB file into a 256KB extent, you’re reserving four times more space than needed. Later, the system may try to combine (coalesce) nearby small allocations to free up larger contiguous regions. But this cleanup work adds computational cost and can fragment metadata. The main goal of MatBall is to increase the space utilization of SSD partition in the hybrid file system where the entire address space is provided by integrating a small portion of SSD partition with a much larger HDD storage capacity. MatBall tries to consume the remaining spaces as much as possible posterior to file allocation processes, by recursively partitioning segments in the subsequent level and by allowing the further file allocations on the partitioned segments. We evaluated MatBall using IOzone. When file sizes are either a multiple of extent sizes or larger than the extent size, the segment partitioning to the lower level does rarely take place. In this case, the threshold value for the segment partitioning in MatBall does little affect I/O performance. On the other hand, with a large number of small-size files, MatBall can improve I/O bandwidth by converting data into the larger I/O granularity.
